item.title: Saskatchewan Icelandic History Driving Tour — Icelandic Roots
item.description: by Karen Pytlowany and Shaune Jonasson Icelandic settlements in North America progressed west over the years with many settlers filing homestead grants in Saskatchewan. Fewer came directly from Iceland, whereas numerous settlers arrived from the Argyle district in Manitoba, North Dakota and Minnesota. Wherever they moved from, the Icelanders sought a better life here. Many of them found what they wanted in Saskatchewan. You can read about the settlement of Saskatchewan here: Icelandic...

item.title: Dr Sigga Houston - September's Interesting Icelander — Icelandic Roots
item.description: by Shaune Jonasson Our September Interesting Icelander profiles the life and achievements of Sigridur “Sigga” Augusta Christianson Houston, MD. (1893–1996). She was a remarkable pioneer woman in the field of medicine, an era where women were not readily accepted into the profession. She was the first Icelandic-Canadian woman doctor, and the fourth Icelandic woman doctor in the World. Sigga Houston was not an extremist, but rather a woman with conviction and dedication to her profession and...

item.title: Book Club for October 2026 — Icelandic Roots
item.description: by Sharron Arksey The Icelandic Roots Book Club begins a fresh season on October 1 with a new book by a familiar writer. Doreen McFarlane’s most recent book was released earlier this year. Leirárskotta: Memoirs of an Icelandic Immigrant Ghost profiles the family ghost that has both tormented and protected Doreen’s family for eight generations, first in Iceland and later in North America. item.title: Icelandic Settlements - The Saskatchewan Story — Icelandic Roots
item.description: by Shaune Jonasson Settling the untamed land of the Canadian prairie, originally known as Assiniboia in the North-West Territories (NWT) before Saskatchewan was a province in 1905, was fulfilled by many ethnicities, including our Icelandic ancestors. Filing for homesteads, then carving out a living in this vast open land was no small feat.
